global-economics-3f7cbd5398.headline: Jensen Huang controversy triggers fresh US push to block advanced AI chip exports to China — Report
global-economics-3f7cbd5398.fulltext:
Written By Ravi HariPublished15 Nov 2026, 06:28 PM IST
US lawmakers are stepping up efforts to restrict the export of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, with allegations surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang adding fresh momentum to a bipartisan push for tighter controls, the Financial Times reported.
Democrats and Republicans are reportedly backing a series of legislative proposals aimed at curbing overseas sales of sensitive semiconductor technology and giving Congress greater powers to review and potentially block export deals already approved by the Donald Trump administration.
The renewed push comes amid controversy surrounding Huang, who had extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. The woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer that has been under US investigation for more than a year over suspected chip smuggling to China, according to the FT.
"There’s absolutely increased momentum for this legislation in light of the recent scandal," FT quoted Owen Tedford, a senior research analyst at Washington-based Beacon Research, as saying.
"Nvidia may feel like they’re done or trying to move on, but Washington is not ready to move on," Tedford added.
Huang had previously pushed for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports.
Several bills under consideration in Congress seek to tighten restrictions on the overseas sale and use of advanced AI chips.
One of the proposals, the Remote Access Security Act, seeks to prevent Chinese companies from remotely accessing advanced chips located overseas through cloud computing services, even when those companies are prohibited from purchasing the physical hardware, the news outlet said.
The proposed legislation is aimed at closing a potential loophole in existing US export controls, which restrict the direct sale of certain advanced chips to Chinese entities but may not adequately address access through overseas computing infrastructure.
Supporters of tighter export controls reportedly argue that restricting China's access to this technology is critical to preserving America's technological and national security advantages.
Three senior Republican lawmakers have called for immediate action on legislation aimed at strengthening congressional oversight of advanced semiconductor exports.
John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford, who chair House committees overseeing China, foreign affairs and intelligence, respectively, wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department official overseeing export controls.
They requested, as per the report, that the three appear before Congress to explain the circumstances surrounding the chip exports and the potential national security implications.
"We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the lawmakers wrote.
They also argued that the controversy demonstrated why Congress needed to pass four bills aimed at strengthening oversight of sensitive technology exports.
The lawmakers' intervention comes as questions mount over how Nvidia chips were allowed to reach Megaspeed despite concerns about the company's alleged involvement in diverting advanced semiconductors to China.
The proposed restrictions could gain a significant legislative boost if lawmakers attach them to the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
The NDAA is a major piece of legislation that authorises funding and policy priorities for the US Department of Defense. It is considered a must-pass bill, making it a potentially effective vehicle for incorporating other legislative measures.
According to the FT, several of the proposed chip export restrictions have received support from outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson and Hakeem Jeffries, who is seen as his likely successor.
Lawmakers are reportedly negotiating the final version of the annual defence legislation, with the possibility of incorporating the new export-control measures into the package.
The current Republican-majority Congress is expected to consider the NDAA before lawmakers elected in the November midterm elections take their seats in January.
The renewed congressional push has also placed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under pressure to explain how Nvidia was allowed to sell chips to Megaspeed.
Under US export-control rules, American companies need licences from the Commerce Department to export certain goods to entities included on the government's so-called Entity List.
The controversy has raised questions about the effectiveness of the existing licensing and enforcement framework, particularly when it comes to preventing advanced AI chips from being diverted to restricted destinations.
Lawmakers are seeking greater oversight of export approvals, including the ability to examine and potentially block transactions that have already received administration clearance.

india-0c884ffd90.headline: India, U.S. agreed on preferential market access for Indian goods in America: Goyal
india-0c884ffd90.fulltext:
India and the U.S. have already agreed that Indian goods in the American market will receive preferential market access compared to competitor nations, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Sunday (November 15, 2026).
India and the U.S. finalised the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February.
The deal was to be signed earlier, but changes in the U.S. tariff landscape have led to further negotiations on the agreement.
“This was already agreed between the leaders — President [Donald] Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi — when they announced that we have both come to a broad framework agreement a few months ago and it has been acknowledged that India will get preferential trade access in the U.S. with lower duties than our competitor countries,” Mr. Goyal told reporters in Cairo.
He is in Cairo on a two-day visit to discuss ways to boost trade and investment between India and Egypt.
The Minister was replying to a question about the U.S. assurance that Indian goods will get preferential market access.
An official has recently stated that the U.S. has assured India of a comparative tariff advantage over competing countries under the proposed bilateral trade agreement (BTA), with both sides working to conclude the first tranche by the end of the current financial year.
“We will have to see how the tariff framework unfolds. We are working towards closing the first tranche by the end of this financial year. Talks are going for the first tranche and the broader BTA,” the official said last week.
The extent of the advantage to Indian goods, however, will depend on the tariff framework eventually agreed upon.
After the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Mr. Trump’s reciprocal tariffs that were the basis of negotiations, the U.S. is using alternative mechanisms to put up a new tariff architecture in place using provisions of the Trade Act.

ai-fa232e2aaf.headline: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
ai-fa232e2aaf.fulltext:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.
The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.
The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.
The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.
In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

ai-a04aaf1b9d.headline: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
ai-a04aaf1b9d.fulltext:
Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
AI has barely displaced any jobs in Australia so far, but young workers entering highly exposed fields like software development are faring worse.
An analysis by Mike Major for Australia's central bank (RBA) built a monitoring system that focuses on the areas where effects are likely to appear first, namely entry-level workers and highly AI-exposed occupations such as programming, clerical work, and customer service.
According to the analysis, job postings have fallen across all groups since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, with the steepest drop in the highest-exposure group. In that group, workers aged 15 to 24 and young college graduates have weaker employment rates and higher unemployment than older workers.
Major cautions against drawing early conclusions, since the study does not establish direct causation and measures only theoretical exposure, not actual use by companies. Post-pandemic shifts in the business cycle or in remote work could also be driving the numbers. According to SEEK data, AI is complementing existing work while also creating new demand for AI skills.
Other studies paint a similar picture, with caveats
An August 2025 Stanford study based on millions of US payroll records found a similar pattern, with employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations down 13 percent in relative terms since late 2022 and nearly 20 percent among young software developers. More experienced workers in the same occupations held steady or gained ground.
A March 2026 Anthropic study also found signs of declining hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed occupations, with job-finding rates down about 14 percent. It found no systematic rise in overall unemployment, however. Theoretical automation potential and actual AI use are far apart, according to the study.
Anthropic offers a company-level example. According to an internal review, the share of junior hires in technical roles has fallen from 27 percent to 9 percent since early 2025. In August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as human employees. Anthropic concedes that, as an extremely AI-intensive software company, it is a special case. Even so, researchers warn of a "tragedy of the cognitive commons", in which disappearing junior roles lead to a future shortage of experienced professionals, assuming those professionals are still needed.
A large study of 25,000 workers in Denmark confirms the lack of economy-wide impact. Despite a 64 percent AI adoption rate, researchers found no measurable changes in wages or hours worked. Workers saved an average of just 2.8 percent of their working time.
A January 2026 analysis of 10.6 million LinkedIn profiles and US unemployment data, however, cautions against blaming the downturn on AI alone. The research team led by Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh found that the problems in exposed occupations started in early 2022, months before ChatGPT launched. Macroeconomic factors like the Fed's shift in interest rate policy or a correction after pandemic-era hiring surges may play a bigger role than previously assumed.
At the same time, AI is creating new demand. According to the World Economic Forum's "Future of Jobs Report 2025", 77 percent of surveyed companies are prioritizing upskilling over job cuts. WEF researchers project a net gain of 78 million jobs by 2030. According to LinkedIn, AI-related job postings grew sixfold in one year.

global-economics-8154b354b3.headline: IIFCL tightens loan terms as Yotta's debt tops $1.4 billion
global-economics-8154b354b3.fulltext:
Hiranandani Group’s Yotta Data Services has secured a ₹2,948-crore ($315 million) loan from state-owned India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd (IIFCL) to build its single largest data centre in Noida. But the 15-year loan comes with some caveats – the lender wants the promoter to eventually own the Nvidia chips deployed at the facility.
This comes amid Yotta’s growing debt as the company expands its data centre infrastructure and capacity. Its total long-term borrowings crossed $1.4 billion with the fresh IIFCL loan.
Documents filed by Yotta with the corporate affairs ministry showed that the Noida ‘D2’ data centre has an estimated project cost of ₹3,879 crore. The promoters of the firm are expected to fund the remaining ₹931 crore beyond IIFCL’s loan that Yotta has secured.
A spokesperson for Yotta confirmed the funding details to Mint, saying the facility will add 61 megawatt (MW) of data processing capacity.
IIFCL, however, appears to be tightening the noose around Yotta. As per the loan documents reviewed by Mint, while Yotta will initially rent out Nvidia’s B300 graphic processing units (GPUs) to run AI workloads from London-based IT firm Gorilla Technology Group, these chips will have to be eventually purchased by Darshan Hiranandani, promoter of Yotta.
The promoter will also have to fund any additional amount required to purchase an equivalent quantity of Nvidia GPUs, under the loan conditions, as per the lending document dated 9 September.
The clause to enforce ownership of Nvidia chips with Yotta’s promoters was framed in a way to allow IIFCL to seize the chips if Yotta defaults in payments.
Yotta will also have to show proof of securing clients for its data centre to IIFCL to receive the final 20% of the approved funds.
The company defended the conditions, saying “milestone-linked disbursement is the standard architecture of infrastructure lending in India: funds are released as the project is built and as the arrangements that will generate its revenue are put in place.”
“Aligning the final tranche with the deployment arrangements for the facility's GPU capacity is a prudent structure that Yotta welcomes,” it added.
Debt mounts
The fund-raise comes as part of Yotta’s efforts to raise up to $1.5 billion this fiscal year, including a $400 million public listing by March 2027, its cofounder and chief executive, Sunil Gupta told Mint in August.
Lenders and credit rating agencies, however, flagged Yotta’s growing debt. In July, credit rating agency Crisil said Yotta’s external debt stood at ₹7,509 crore as of March 2026, besides ₹3,031 crore owed to suppliers and contractors. The agency warned that debt could reach up to ₹12,000 crore by March 2027 without fresh equity to reduce borrowings.
With IIFCL’s fund-raise, Yotta’s net long-term borrowings stand at ₹13,488 crore (over $1.4 billion).
Besides IIFCL, Yotta’s lenders include SBI, Indian Bank, Bank of Maharashtra and Axis Bank, according to India Ratings’ bank-wise disclosures.
The company reported ₹890.7 crore in operating revenue in FY25, with FY26 financials yet to be filed.
In a 28 July report, India Ratings flagged a separate concern: the difference between the tenure of Yotta's debt and the commercial life of its GPU business.
“Weighted average debt tenure in excess of 10 years is long as against the shorter contract tenure and lifespan for GPU business remains a risk and requires monitoring,” it said.
This means Yotta could still be repaying loans long after its AI chips become outdated.
The spokesperson said its borrowings have increased alongside its assets and revenue from customer contracts.
“The 10-year infrastructure loan is not being serviced from short GPU contracts; it is serviced by the facility, which will host successive generations of equipment over its life,” the spokesperson said. “The IIFCL facility finances the data-centre infrastructure: the building, power, cooling and connectivity. The GPUs to be deployed at D2 are financed separately through third-party equipment financing, which is the structure Yotta uses across its campuses.”
Government-owned IIFCL lends to projects across sectors including roads, airports, power and data centres. It reported ₹6,723.6 crore in FY25 revenue, up 13%, and ₹2,631.4 crore in net profit, up 61%. The company mainly makes money by charging interest on loans given to infrastructure projects.
Yotta is one of the many companies ramping up borrowings to fund capital-intensive data centre build-outs which promise to rake in billions in revenue over years to come.
India’s data centre capacity is expected to more than triple to 5.6 gigawatt (GW) by 2030, from 1.8GW in June this year per an 8 September estimate by real estate consultant Cushman & Wakefield, driven by rising demand for cloud services and AI applications.

indian-startups-6373036a72.headline: Sebi to issue AI usage guidelines for capital markets, focus on investor protection
indian-startups-6373036a72.fulltext:
Sebi to issue AI usage guidelines for capital markets, focus on investor protection
The Sebi chief said the proposed guidelines would focus on establishing appropriate guardrails for AI use, including disclosures, accountability of regulated entities, and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach.
Markets regulator Sebi will soon issue detailed guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the capital markets, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said, emphasising the need to balance technological innovation with investor protection.
The Sebi chief said the proposed guidelines would focus on establishing appropriate guardrails for AI use, including disclosures, accountability of regulated entities and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach to ensure that critical decisions are subject to human oversight.
In June 2025, Sebi (Securities and Exchange Board of India) floated a consultation paper proposing guiding principles for responsible usage of artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications/models in securities markets.
These guiding principles are intended to optimise benefits and minimise potential risks associated with the integration of AI/ML based applications in securities markets to safeguard investor protection, market integrity, and financial stability.
Speaking at the inauguration of Sebi's pavilion at the 45th India International Trade Fair 2026, organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation, on Saturday, Pandey said the regulator has been continuously strengthening its cybersecurity framework to address rising cyber threats.
He highlighted growing concerns over cyberattacks targeting financial institutions and cryptocurrency platforms, as well as digital frauds involving social media influencers.
Following emerging threats, the regulator also introduced a structured incident response mechanism in May this year, aligned with the Financial Stability Board's FIRE reporting template, he said at the sidelines of an event here on Saturday.
On quantum computing-related risks, the Chairman said Sebi is undertaking an inventory of cryptographic systems and identifying areas where cryptography is being used to assess potential vulnerabilities.
He said markets globally are preparing for the risks posed by quantum computing, with concerns expected to become more pronounced around 2032-35, and stressed the need to complete preparations well in advance.
On AI adoption, he said Sebi has also developed several supervisory tools, including its 'Sudarshan' tool, which is being demonstrated at international regulatory forums.
The regulator is also working on strengthening its AI capabilities through international initiatives and supervisory toolkits, he added.
The Chairman further said Sebi is reviewing the regulatory framework to ensure that the use of AI by market participants does not compromise investor protection, market safety or integrity.
On startups and the listing framework, the Sebi chief also said the regulator has formed a working group to examine ways to make the Innovators Growth Platform (IGP) more attractive for startups, particularly deep-tech and biotech companies that require long gestation periods before generating profits.
He said the existing platform has not gained the desired traction, and the regulator is reviewing potential changes to help such companies access public markets at an earlier stage.
The objective is to provide investors clarity about the higher risks associated with such businesses while allowing them to participate in their long-term growth potential.
However, he declined to share details of budget-related discussions.

world-e56b32999e.headline: Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
world-e56b32999e.fulltext:
Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.
Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.
The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.
He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine,” Michal said.
“Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine.”
The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company that authorities have attributed to Russia, after an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.
In September, Kapo said it was confident that the incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”.
The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.
At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.
Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks on defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries – on online messaging platforms – to carry out acts of sabotage.
Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.
The Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, told state news agency Tass: “If these [border closures] are their real plans, then they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia.”

climate-energy-71f8eada76.headline: India Bans Lithium-Ion Battery Black Mass Exports: What It Means For EV Battery Recycling
climate-energy-71f8eada76.fulltext:
The move is aimed at securing domestic feedstock for battery recyclers and recovering valuable minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel. However, building the capacity to process this material into usable battery-grade products remains the bigger challenge
                        
India has stopped the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, a material recovered from discarded batteries that contains valuable minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and energy storage systems. The move is aimed at ensuring that these resources are processed within the country instead of being shipped overseas.
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), through Notification No. 49/2026-27 dated November 10, 2026, has changed the export policy for black mass under ITC (HS) Code 85491400 from 'Free' to 'Prohibited', with immediate effect and until further orders.
The decision is significant for India's battery recycling industry. The government says that while domestic recycling and mineral recovery capacity has increased, it is not being fully utilised because of inadequate feedstock availability. In some cases, Indian recyclers have even had to import black mass to meet their processing requirements, while material generated within the country was being exported.
The restriction is intended to address this mismatch by retaining domestically generated black mass for local recycling and refining.
What Exactly Is Black Mass And Why Is It Valuable?
Black mass is a dark, powder-like material obtained by shredding and processing used lithium-ion batteries, including end-of-life EV batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable quantities of several critical minerals, including:
- Lithium: Used in the production of lithium-ion battery cells.
- Cobalt: Used in certain battery chemistries to improve stability and performance.
- Nickel: Helps improve battery energy density.
- Manganese: Used in several cathode chemistries.
These minerals can be recovered from black mass through further processing and used as inputs for battery manufacturing. This makes discarded batteries an important secondary source of materials that India otherwise depends substantially on imports for.
In simple terms, black mass is not the finished battery material. It is an intermediate resource containing valuable metals that need to be separated, refined and converted into usable compounds.
What Does The DGFT Notification Prohibit?
The restriction applies to the material classified under ITC (HS) Code 85491400. The tariff classification covers unsorted waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, including spent cells and batteries that do not contain lead, cadmium or mercury. The notification specifically identifies lithium-ion battery black mass.
The notification also provides for transitional arrangements under Paragraph 1.05 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023. Under these provisions, certain export commitments backed by irrevocable commercial letters of credit issued before the restriction may qualify for transitional relief, subject to prescribed conditions, including registration with the jurisdictional DGFT regional authority within 15 days.
The notification is specifically directed at the identified battery waste and black mass category. It should not be interpreted as a blanket prohibition on exports of finished batteries or all refined critical mineral products.
Can Domestic Recyclers Handle The Additional Material?
This is where the policy change will face its biggest test. According to reports, 57 lithium-ion battery recyclers registered on the Central Pollution Control Board's Battery Waste Extended Producer Responsibility portal have a combined annual processing capacity of 5.17 lakh metric tonnes. However, the estimated input capacity of companies specifically processing lithium-ion battery black mass is around 75,500 metric tonnes annually.
These are different capacity measures, the larger figure refers to registered lithium-ion battery recycling capacity, while the smaller one relates specifically to units processing black mass.
The distinction matters because collecting and shredding used batteries is only one part of the recycling process. Recovering lithium, cobalt, nickel and other materials to the purity levels required by manufacturers involves more specialised technology, investment and processing capabilities. The export restriction can improve the availability of raw material for domestic recyclers, but it cannot by itself guarantee that the recovered minerals will meet the quality and scale required by battery manufacturers.
There is also an economic question. If recyclers cannot process black mass efficiently or secure buyers for the recovered materials, simply retaining it within the country will not deliver the intended benefits.
Part Of India's Larger Critical Mineral Strategy
The decision comes amid a wider government effort to develop domestic capabilities across the critical mineral supply chain. In September 2025, the Union Cabinet approved a Rs 1,500-crore Incentive Scheme for Promotion of Critical Mineral Recycling. The scheme is part of the National Critical Mineral Mission and aims to support the recovery of critical minerals from secondary sources, including spent lithium-ion batteries, electronic waste and other scrap. 
More recently, on November 4, 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a separate Rs 2,814-crore capital expenditure support scheme for critical mineral processing. It will run from FY2026-27 to FY2030-31 and provide a 30 per cent capital subsidy for four proposed processing plants - two lithium plants with a minimum capacity of 30,000 tonnes each and two nickel plants with a minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes each.
The newer scheme focuses on processing lithium and nickel ores or intermediary products into high-purity materials, with cobalt expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production. It is therefore a broader processing initiative, separate from the Rs 1,500-crore recycling incentive scheme.
Together, these measures indicate a push to develop more domestic sources of critical minerals, whether through recycling discarded batteries or processing mineral-bearing raw materials.
The Real Objective Is To Close The Battery Recycling Loop
India's battery manufacturing ambitions will require reliable access to lithium, nickel, cobalt and other materials. At present, the country remains substantially dependent on imports for several of these resources and for their refined intermediates.
Recycling offers an opportunity to recover some of these materials from batteries that have reached the end of their useful life. It can also reduce the need to depend entirely on newly mined resources.
The export prohibition is therefore an attempt to retain more value within India's domestic supply chain. But the outcome will depend on whether recycling companies can expand their processing capabilities, recover minerals economically and supply battery manufacturers with materials that meet quality requirements. Keeping black mass in India is the first step. Turning it into usable critical minerals at commercial scale is the challenge that follows.

ai-68dce59598.headline: Firm linked to Jensen Huang's ex-lover reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for China
ai-68dce59598.fulltext:
Firm linked to Jensen Huang's ex-lover reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for China
Update:
In a statement to Reuters, Megaspeed said Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang officially left the company on August 30, 2025, and has no current role there. Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS. The company said it conducted "legitimate and lawful business" and had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.
The New York Times reported in October 2025 that Megaspeed was under investigation over whether it helped Chinese customers obtain export-controlled Nvidia chips. There has also been speculation that Alice Huang may be a Chinese spy, which has not been confirmed.
Original article, November 15, 2026:
Megaspeed arranged nearly $12 billion worth of Nvidia high-performance chip orders for Chinese companies between March 2024 and June 2025, according to documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal. The company is owned by Alice Huang, the former lover of since-ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Megaspeed shipped the chips to buyers in China who maintained long-standing business ties with local tech giants, the WSJ reports. ai-2f404cbfd4.headline: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
ai-2f404cbfd4.fulltext:
Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.
A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.
The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.
The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.
The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.
Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.
“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”
A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.
IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.
The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.
Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.
It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.
Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.
The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.
Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.
“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”
Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.
“We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. But there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse. We have the knowledge and tools to make a difference.
“We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

india-deep-tech-bfd03d5b4d.headline: Inside Pakistan’s air-to-air missile arsenal: From Chinese PL-15s to indigenous Fa’az
india-deep-tech-bfd03d5b4d.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-bfd03d5b4d.fulltext:
New Delhi: Pakistan recently flight-tested its first indigenously developed air-to-air missile (AAM), named Fa’az (Urdu for victorious). The development marks a significant step for the country, which has so far relied primarily on Chinese- and US-made missiles. For India, the development merits attention, as recent standoffs between the two countries have been characterised by aerial engagements and Pakistan could potentially use the missile for a future conflict.
On 3 November, the day of the test, Pakistan military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, “The successful flight test underscores the technical maturity, innovation and self-reliance achieved by Pakistan’s defence industry.”
A video released by Pakistan showed the missile fitted onto a JF-17 Thunder, the fighter aircraft jointly developed by Pakistan and China.
Equipped with a state-of-the-art terminal guidance system, Fa’az is designed to engage enemy aerial targets at longer ranges, placing it in the category of Beyond-Visual-Range Air-to-Air Missiles (BVRAAMs). Importantly, the missile shown in the video was the passive imaging infrared (IIR) version, known as Fa’az IIR. A separate active radar-guided (RF) variant is also under development.
IIR missiles are tactically more effective as they use thermal imaging to build a two-dimensional image or silhouette of the target before locking on, rather than relying primarily on the heat signature of the target as older infrared (IR) missiles do.
The Fa’az IIR has an estimated detection range of 40 kilometres, while the RF version has a detection range of 25 km. Both variants are projected to have a range exceeding 100 km and a maximum speed of Mach 3.5 (supersonic).
The missile is being developed under Pakistan’s National Engineering and Scientific Commission (NESCOM) by the state-owned defence conglomerate Global Industrial and Defence Solutions (GIDS). The company first showcased mock-ups of both Fa’az variants at a defence exhibition in Istanbul, Turkey, in 2023. GIDS maintains that its products are developed locally and that it owns their intellectual property rights.
Pakistan has not released detailed information about Fa’az’s flight test or disclosed the development status of its radar-guided RF variant. Regardless of when the missile enters operational service, the test marks a significant step for Pakistan’s air defence industry.
Writing for The War Zone, a defence and military analysis website, Thomas Newdick described it as “a significant development in the country’s efforts to establish a domestic air-to-air weapons capability and join a relatively small group of countries with the expertise to develop such weapons”.
Also Read: Why Pakistan’s veteran power broker Maulana Fazlur Rehman is now challenging the military
Moving beyond American and Chinese missiles
Air Marshal Diptendu Choudhury (Retd), an airpower specialist and author affiliated with several Indian think-tanks, told ThePrint that Pakistan was dependent on the US for long, but started looking to China after America imposed sanctions on the sale of F-16s to Islamabad in 1990. “The Chinese helped Pakistan with technology, while Pakistan assisted the Chinese air force in expanding its operational experience by way of bilateral joint exercises like Shaheen.” He added that there were limits to the extent of China’s assistance, prompting Pakistan to move towards self-reliance.
Beyond reducing dependence on foreign suppliers, greater domestic production could also allow Pakistan to export its weapons systems. Fa’az could complement the JF-17 Thunder, which Pakistan is already exporting, giving prospective buyers the option of acquiring both the fighter aircraft and its accompanying air-to-air missile.
However, Air Marshal AK Bharti, Director General of Air Operations during Operation Sindoor, questioned Pakistan’s claim that the missile was indigenous. “The indigenous component of Fa’az should be taken with a pinch of salt, as they could very well just be assembling foreign components,” he told ThePrint.
Foreign technological influences in Pakistan’s indigenous missile inventory cannot be ruled out, given Islamabad’s longstanding defence ties with China. GIDS is also developing a longer-range missile, called Fa’az-2, in technological cooperation with Turkey’s TÜBİTAK SAGE, which is developing the country’s own air-to-air missile, GÖKDOĞAN.
Air Marshal Bharti said India should take note of the development regardless of how much of the missile is indigenous. “It is a capability with the adversary, however small it may be,” he said.
Recent clashes between India and Pakistan have predominantly involved beyond-visual-range (BVR) engagements. A defining feature of Operation Sindoor was that aircraft from neither India nor Pakistan crossed into each other’s airspace and the fighting occurred through long-range and BVR platforms.
“The next India-Pakistan standoff, as indeed an aerial battle anywhere in the world, would predominantly be a BVR combat, but you cannot do away with within-visual-range AAMs (WVRAAMs) completely,” Air Marshal Bharti told ThePrint.
Against this backdrop, it is important to take stock of the PAF’s existing BVRAAM inventory.
PL-12/SD-10A
Among the longer-range missiles in Pakistan’s inventory is the Chinese SD-10A BVRAAM, an export variant of the PL-12 missile. It is produced under licence by the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex and appears to have partly influenced Fa’az’s design.
A report by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) said the PL-12 was China’s first indigenous active radar-guided air-to-air missile. It entered service with the Chinese Air Force and Navy in 2005.
The SD-10A is an active radar-guided BVRAAM fitted on Chinese combat aircraft, including the JF-17 Thunder. Its range is slightly lower than that of the PL-12 which, according to many estimates, has a maximum range of 100 km, with the export version having a maximum range of roughly 70 km.
PL-15E and Operation Sindoor
Another long-range missile in Pakistan’s inventory is the Chinese PL-15E, the export variant of the PL-15. It is integrated into the armament of the J-10C and JF-17 Block III fighters.
Designed as an advanced successor to the PL-12, the PL-15 is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar seeker. It is powered by a dual-pulse solid rocket motor and has a maximum speed of Mach 4–5 (supersonic).
The RUSI report notes that the PL-15 has a profile visually similar to the US-made AIM-120 C/D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM), but “outranges the latest AIM-120D model and has a comparable maximum range to the Meteor [French-made missile]”.
Pakistan was the first export customer for the PL-15E. Its first deployment came during the May 2025 confrontation with India, following the Pahalgam attack. Missile debris reportedly fell inside Indian territory in Hoshiarpur, Punjab. Air Marshal AK Bharti subsequently confirmed at a press briefing following Operation Sindoor that Pakistan had used the missile, pointing to its debris.
The PL-15E’s operational range caught the Indian Air Force (IAF) off guard, according to a Reuters report. Indian officials had estimated its range at approximately 150 km. The missile, however, struck an Indian aircraft from a distance of nearly 200 km during combat, Reuters reported.
American AAMs
For its fleet of American F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft, Pakistan relies on US-made AAMs, particularly the AIM-120C-5 AMRAAM. According to data from one of its operators, the AIM-120C-5 has a maximum range of around 74 km.
During the 2019 India-Pakistan confrontation following the Pulwama attack, India publicly displayed debris from an AIM-120C-5 as evidence that Pakistan had deployed its American-made F-16s against India.
“Pakistan claimed they did not use F-16. There is enough evidence to show that F-16s were used in this mission through their electronic signatures. Parts of AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is carried only on the F-16s, was recovered east of Rajouri within Indian territory,” Air Vice Marshal R.G.K. Kapoor had said after the 2019 confrontation.
Air Marshal Diptendu Choudhury said the US had refused to acknowledge that Pakistan used F-16s against India, given Islamabad’s assurances that the aircraft would be used for counter-terrorism operations rather than against India.
Months after Operation Sindoor, the US confirmed the sale of AMRAAMs to Pakistan through defence manufacturer Raytheon. On 30 September 2025, the US Department of War issued a press release announcing contracts awarded to several American defence firms. The US Embassy in India subsequently confirmed the sale, but described it not as a new agreement to upgrade Pakistan’s existing capabilities, but as “an existing Foreign Military Sales contract for sustainment and spares for several countries, including Pakistan”.
Pakistan had earlier purchased 700 AAMs from US-based Raytheon in 2007. The order included 500 AMRAAMs, making it the largest international order for the weapon at the time, and 200 short-range AIM-9M Sidewinder missiles.
The bigger question here is whether Pakistan would deploy its American AMRAAM (and its F-16 fleet at large) against India again, even though the PAF’s large inventory of Chinese-AAMs provides enough alternatives to bypass American systems against India.
French and American short-range AAMs
The infrared-guided Sidewinder remains a short-range weapon of choice for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet. The PAF continues to operate the all-aspect AIM-9L and the older AIM-9P variants.
It also operates the French-made, infrared-guided Matra Magic 2 AAM, which is comparable to the AIM-9L and offers an alternative to the US-made weapon.
These short-range AAMs (SRAAMs) are primarily intended for within-visual-range (WVR) dogfights. Given the changing nature of aerial combat and the growing importance of BVRAAMs, their role in a future India-Pakistan confrontation may be more limited.
Implications for India
Air Marshal AK Bharti told ThePrint that India should take note of the development without being unduly alarmed. “Any new weapon the adversary gets will naturally be a cause of concern, but India need not be unduly alarmed by this development. Of course, India must continue to keep its eyes open and factor in each and every development across the border, in its larger scheme of things,” he said.
Given Pakistan’s asymmetry with India and its continued reliance on foreign suppliers, maintaining a substantial stockpile of AAMs remains critical for Islamabad. However, dependence on other countries poses both financial and geopolitical constraints and indigenous production could reduce the risk of the PAF depleting its BVRAAM supplies in the case of a prolonged conflict with India.
Air Marshal Choudhury said that, over and above the radar range, the missile’s range should be greater than the adversary’s. “India for the longest time, up until the Kargil war, had a BVR missile advantage over Pakistan. This advantage lay in the Indian Air Force’s AAM ability to outstick PAF’s.”
Put simply, the IAF’s missiles had a greater range than Pakistan’s weapons. By the 2019 Balakot strikes, however, Pakistan possessed more sophisticated AMRAAMs than India’s, the Air Marshal said.
India has its own indigenous BVRAAM family, Astra, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). The Astra Mk-1, with a range exceeding 100 kilometres, has already been inducted into the IAF. Its range is being extended, while the Astra Mk-2 is undergoing testing. Plans are also underway for the Astra Mk-3.
So, while Fa’az expanded the weapons options available to its Air Force, what will ultimately matter is whether Pakistan can match or exceed Indian missile ranges and how quickly it can produce and induct the missile into operational service.

Ukraine's robots are increasingly able to down aerial drones, a capability that could eventually help soldiers move and fight in some of the war's most dangerous areas.

"
With effective protection against those drones, he said, "the nature of combat operations along the line of contact could change substantially."
He called defending the "low sky" by countering enemy drones a promising role for ground robots.
Beyond leading front-line operators, Yabchanka also co-founded Defence Robotics UA, a non-profit that helps Ukrainian units adopt robotic technologies.
"I have particularly high hopes for the use of ground-based robotic systems in defending the low-altitude airspace," he said.
The kill zone
Inside the kill zone, drones complicate movement, so robots are taking on new roles in logistics, casualty evacuation, and more. Some of these systems are equipped with weaponry and jamming equipment to take down hostile drones.
Robots equipped for counter-drone missions could reduce the demand for short-range air defense units, which provide cover for infantry moving in and out, in the kill zone. Right now, these units face great danger and risk getting pinned down inside.
These robots could also defend themselves as Russia increasingly targets them.
Mykyta Rozhkov, chief business development officer at Ukrainian robotics and technology company Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that robots are "becoming a main target" for Russia and are defenseless without added protections.
Giving robots the ability to defend themselves could make them more survivable, while turning them into mobile air defenses could help protect troops.
Rozhkov said makers are now "trying to find a way how we can defend against FPVs."
Yabchanka said that when it comes to changing the kill zone, "it would be incorrect to promise that this will happen specifically within the next 12 months."
But he said robots have already successfully stopped some drones, and "I believe this field has a great future."
Robots vs drones
Most of the technology in this space is still being tested or used on a limited scale, primarily to protect the robots themselves rather than provide broader air defense.
Rozhkov said that while it's key to have uncrewed ground vehicles be capable of defending themselves, he expects to eventually see UGVs functioning as a mobile, short-range air defense system to try to clear the skies.
His company is working with a partner on a system that uses cameras and sensors to find hostile drones and then engages them with a separate capability. He didn't disclose how it would engage enemy drones.
Other Ukrainian robot makers are also adding anti-drone capabilities, some involving smoke, nets, and shrapnel solutions. Robots are increasingly being fitted with weaponry like machine guns, and some companies have said that these weapons can stop enemy drones.
Ukrainian company UFORCE, for instance, says it has destroyed enemy drones in ambush scenarios. The company's AI-assisted Predator weapons station can be mounted on robots to track and fire at drones. The 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade previously described a machine gun mounted on a Liut robot shooting down Russian drones.
Rovertech, which advertises itself as making "robots for the kill zone," is developing a system that uses sensors, AI-assisted detection, and a net launcher to stop incoming drones, while Ratel Robotics has started serial production on a protective system that includes net launchers on its robots.
Ukraine's 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade said last month that it had deployed an active protection system using net launchers and shared a video showing one of its robots firing a net at an approaching drone, which then crashed to the ground.
Some Ukrainian units have also driven robots carrying electronic warfare equipment forward to jam Russia's drones, but it's an emerging capability that has yet to see widespread use.
Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, says armed robots are starting to be used against aerial drones, but it wants more, describing anti-aircraft weaponry and protection as priorities.
Rozhkov said that soon, Ukraine's robots will have "more and more sophisticated solutions" to stop drones.
He said it's essential because the first side that figures out how to stop small FPVs "will gain a huge advantage on the battlefield and can create dramatic results."

climate-energy-85a5e65e5f.fulltext:
The planned network would be India’s highest-voltage transmission system, reports said, at an estimated cost of about 68,800 crore rupees.
India’s national transmission panel has approved a 1,150-kV transmission corridor linking the western and eastern regions, according to minutes released late Tuesday, Nov. 10. The project is estimated to cost nearly ₹68,800 crore and take about six years to complete.
The network would carry more power than the current system. The proposed 1,150-kV network offers substantially higher transmission capability compared to the existing 765-kV system, and it minimizes the need for multiple EHV transmission corridors.
ALSO READ: India-Germany Energy Cooperation
Why the 1,150-kV Network Reduces Transmission
The ultra-high-voltage 1,150-kV transmission corridor will lower transmission losses, optimise right-of-way land use, and avoid the need for multiple parallel lines. Operating at 1,150 kV instead of 765 kV reduces the electrical current required to carry the same quantum of power, cutting resistive conductor losses while planners factor in 660-MVAr reactors to manage reactive compensation and line charging.
Route, Capacity, and Phased Implementation Timeline
The first phase would link Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and West Bengal. It would also connect with a 6,000-megawatt high-voltage transmission system carrying renewable power from Rajasthan’s Bhadla solar region. Government minutes from September describe that link as a 800-kilovolt, 6,000-megawatt HVDC line from Bhadla-IV to Raigarh Kotra-III.
The combined length of the corridor over both phases will reach around 3,750 circuit-kilometers with transformation capacity of 66,000 megavolt-amperes, the September minutes noted. Early planning papers refer to a six-year timeframe. Phase II shall be implemented in a phased manner based on the suggestions received from GRID-INDIA depending upon the real rise in load in Odisha and Maharashtra.
ALSO READ: Green Targets
Industrial Decarbonisation and Green Hydrogen Demand
The 1,150-kV transmission corridor is designed to move power from western states such as Rajasthan toward growing industrial demand in the east, including Odisha. In eastern India, the corridor is geared toward powering upcoming green hydrogen, green ammonia, steel, petrochemical, solar PV, and EV manufacturing hubs in Odisha, particularly around Paradeep and Gopalpur.
The Central Electricity Authority noted that about 12 gigawatts of green hydrogen and green ammonia demand was considered, while the modeled loading on the corridor was about 3 to 3.5 gigawatts. Grid planners including GRID-INDIA and GETCO have flagged that the realisation of projected green hydrogen loads remains uncertain, making timely industrial connectivity and the completion of the Bhadla-IV HVDC renewable link critical to meeting India’s 2030 non-fossil and green hydrogen targets.

global-economics-5a1970c60d.headline: As inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certain
global-economics-5a1970c60d.fulltext:
The MPC in October had projected the retail-inflation rate at 6 per cent for this quarter and 5.7 per cent for the next. The rate was projected at 5.6 per cent for the first quarter of 2027-28. The latest inflation print has pushed the real repo rate into negative territory, making a policy-rate adjustment necessary. The extent of adjustment in the December meeting and later will depend on several factors, such as the inflation projection for next financial year, prospects of second-order effects through higher food prices, and the level of the real policy rate the central bank is willing to maintain at this stage. 
 An earlier study by RBI economists had estimated the neutral rate — the real policy rate that is neither expansionary nor contractionary— at 1.4-1.9 per cent. It is possible that it has changed. Even assuming that the RBI is comfortable maintaining the real policy rate at 1-1.25 per cent, the repo rate needs to be adjusted by 50-75 basis points, given that the central bank expects the inflation rate to average 5 per cent in 2027-28, according to its latest biannual Monetary Policy Report (October). However, much depends on possible shifts in inflation projections. The monsoon season ended with a rainfall deficit of about 13 per cent as against the long-period average. Given the expected strong El Niño conditions, with adverse implications for rain in winter and lower reservoir levels, agricultural output could also be affected in the rabi season, potentially keeping food prices elevated.
 However, there is some relief, at least for now, on the external front. There are indications that the United States (US) may not resume the Iran war anytime soon, though US action under President Donald Trump remains unpredictable as ever. For now, prices of crude oil have come down significantly. Although gains for India on inflation will remain limited due to the limited pass-through of higher global prices to retail prices, prospects of a lower current-account deficit will support the currency and reduce its impact on inflation outcomes. Lower oil prices and a selloff in artificial intelligence-related stocks in the US have also brought back foreign portfolio investors. While this development will provide stability to the rupee, the RBI will be well advised to use such opportunities to rebuild its foreign-exchange reserves. Stability on the external front will also allow the RBI to focus on inflation management. While the consensus is that the MPC will increase the repo rate by 25 basis points in the December meeting, it may even consider a 50-basis point rate increase to send a strong message, given that growth is not a concern at the moment.

india-d5fce762d2.headline: India's trade deficit with China likely to hit $150 billion in FY27
india-d5fce762d2.fulltext:
With the monthly bilateral trade deficit averaging nearly $12 billion so far this financial year, India’s trade gap with China could balloon to around $150 billion in FY27, compared with $112 billion in FY26, Business Standard calculations show.
 Strong exports to China, at $14 billion during the April-October period, have been driven by growth in marine products (15.84 times), organic chemicals (121 per cent), telecom instruments (96 per cent) and electric machinery and equipment (50 per cent). In contrast, India’s $97 billion imports were led by organic chemicals (52 per cent), electronics components (29 per cent) and telecom instruments (24 per cent).   
 When it comes to individual commodities, India’s top five items exported to China are led by ‘populated, loaded or stuffed’ printed circuit boards, followed by light naphtha, full range naphtha; other telecom equipment parts and Vannamei shrimp. India’s top five imports were other telecom equipment parts, memories /memory chips/, lithium-ion, monolithic integrated circuits (digital) and personal computers (laptops, palmtops etc). 
 India’s surge in electronic exports, especially smartphones, largely relies on China for components, leading to higher imports. India has been pressing China for a long time to facilitate more exports from India, highlighting the unsustainable trade deficit between the two countries. 
 Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman last month said China’s non-tariff barriers were the biggest hurdle for Indian exports, alleging that Beijing had denied market access to Indian products despite significant demand potential for generic drugs, bovine meat and agricultural produce, contributing to a widening trade imbalance. 
 “A decade has gone by consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products, but non-tariff barriers have been very strong, and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly. Non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in trade between India and China,” she said during a conversation hosted by the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. 
 Sitharaman said New Delhi has repeatedly sought market access for products in which India had a competitive advantage, but progress has been limited despite scope for discussions on sanitary and phytosanitary measures and other regulatory issues. 
 Responding to Sitharaman’s remarks, China’s foreign ministry said Beijing was ready to work with New Delhi to address “each other’s economic and trade concerns in a balanced way and promote the steady development of bilateral relations”. “China never aims for trade surplus,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told the media in Beijing. 
 Sitharaman said India has refrained from adopting punitive trade measures to address its trade imbalance with China, preferring negotiations despite the difficulties involved, unlike some other countries. “Probably that’s not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome, but we do go through that approach rather than putting countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter their non-tariff barriers,” she added.

india-625b8dfc3d.headline: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
india-625b8dfc3d.fulltext:
India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
The planned Tamil Nadu yard would expand Korean shipbuilding capacity while helping India pursue its maritime and strategic ambitions.
India’s push to expand domestic shipbuilding and lessen its dependence on China has found an eager partner in Korea, whose shipbuilders are looking for new production bases abroad.
Those complementary needs are driving a burgeoning partnership centered on Thoothukudi, a port city near India's southern tip, where HD Hyundai plans to build a $4 billion shipyard with Indian state partners. On India's west coast, Samsung Heavy Industries is backing an Indian yard competing for the country's first oil tanker orders in decades.
The stakes reach beyond the two countries. China, Korea and Japan accounted for about 93 percent of global shipbuilding in 2024, according to Clarksons Research, and India is spending public money to become the fourth name on that list, with Korean partners instead of Chinese ones.
When India’s shipping minister visited Korea last month, he toured Korean shipyards and explored business opportunities with all three of Korea’s major shipbuilders, underscoring New Delhi’s push to expand its shipbuilding industry.
India’s Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal met HD Hyundai Chairman Chung Ki-sun, Samsung Heavy Industries CEO Choi Sung-an and Hanwha Ocean Executive Vice President Kim Chang-yong to ask for investment and technology transfer during a four-day trip that ended Oct. 28.
The tour was the latest in a series of attempts by New Delhi to import an industry it has not managed to build on its own. India ranks 12th in global shipbuilding and wants to be in the top five by 2047.
For Korean yards that are full at home and losing orders to China, it is a subsidized way to add capacity. The outcome will show whether a shipbuilding industry can be assembled outside East Asia from state funding and borrowed know-how.
Plenty of orders, few yards
About 95 percent of India's trade by volume moves by sea, the country spends close to $75 billion a year hiring foreign ships, and its own yards held 0.5 percent of the global order book as of Sept. 1, according to the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO).
Indian cabinet earmarked 697.3 billion rupees ($7.4 billion) in September 2025 to lift annual capacity to 4.5 million gross tons by 2047. State-run buyers plan to order 437 vessels worth about 2.2 trillion rupees.
Demand is not the constraint but the ability to build is. Indian yards delivered about 65,000 deadweight tons of ships in the fiscal year through March 2025, roughly a fifth of a single supertanker. Cheap labor does not close the gap. An Indian yard needs 150 to 180 man-hours for work that takes 10 to 15 in Korea, Han Seung-han, an analyst at SK Securities, wrote in a September report.
"A policy of adding capacity does not by itself raise the ability to build ships," Han wrote. "The capability to run a yard has to come in whole."
Korean yards face the reverse problem. The industry is in a supercycle, and "domestic production capacity is almost full, with work backed up three to five years," said Lee Kyu-seok, a senior research fellow at the Export-Import Bank of Korea's Overseas Economic Research Institute. India, he added, appears to offer "a structure where it is easier to match production costs."
Nor would Indian yards serve only India. "Shipbuilding is already globalized," Lee said.
A short list of partners
Among the partners India could have chosen, China, the largest builder, seems ruled out. "Because of the border dispute, India does not cooperate with China in strategic industries," said Kim Kyung-hoon, head of the India and South Asia team at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
New Delhi has thawed ties with Beijing, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in September, but relations remain far from the level needed for industrial cooperation, he said. "Handing shipbuilding subsidies to China is unimaginable."
Japan's yards have moved on to high-end vessels, while India wants to start with container ships and bulk carriers, which Korean yards still build, Kim said. "Korea is almost the only partner."
A similar rivalry looks to be pushing Korea toward India. Chinese yards won 63 percent of global new orders last year and Korean yards 21 percent, according to Clarksons Research. Korean builders now see Southeast Asia and India as partners that can help offset China, an industry representative familiar with the matter said.
"After Southeast Asia, India is the market drawing attention," the representative said, adding that India is courting Korea's three major shipbuilders to grow its own industry.
HD Hyundai’s third overseas base
HD Hyundai is leading Korean shipbuilders’ foray into India. When Sonowal met Chung on Oct. 28, the two sides agreed to finish a detailed project report (DPR) on the yard's cost, size and schedule within six months. The local port authority ordered a feasibility study in September, and site inspections are now underway.
HD Hyundai is to run the yard through a joint venture as its largest shareholder. Until it opens, India plans to place its first orders with HD Hyundai's yards in Korea and send workers there for training. The partnership began with a Tamil Nadu state agreement in December 2025.
"The specific shareholding structure and investment size of the joint venture are under discussion with the relevant agencies and partners," HD Hyundai said in a written response to the Korea JoongAng Daily. "However, under the [memorandum of understanding] signed among equity investors on the occasion of the Korea-India summit in April, our baseline is to secure at least 60 percent of the joint venture."
What HD Hyundai gains is scale it cannot add at home. The yard is planned to turn out about 2.5 million gross tons a year, more than half of the capacity India wants nationwide by 2047. It would be the group's third overseas base after Vietnam and the Philippines, and subsidies would carry much of the cost: Han estimates that central and state support will cover 45 to 47 percent of the $4 billion bill, leaving HD Hyundai to fund about $2.2 billion.
"We are looking to build a stable production system by securing both Indian domestic orders and global orders," the company said. "Over the long term, we expect it to diversify our global production system by drawing on India's abundant work force and growth potential, and to complement the production capacity of our domestic yards."
Han expects the next round of global orders to center on tankers and bulk carriers, where competing with China comes down to cost. Nearly half of India's 1,592 ships are more than 20 years old, and most are tankers or bulk carriers, he noted. "It cannot be solved with domestic yards," Han wrote. "The answer is India, following Vietnam and the Philippines."
Samsung Heavy Industries has taken a lighter route, lending know-how to an existing Indian yard instead of building one. It signed a cooperation deal in September 2025 with Swan Defence and Heavy Industries. Last month, Swan submitted the lowest bid for up to four product tankers for a venture led by the state-run Shipping Corporation of India, undercutting a Cochin Shipyard bid backed by HD Hyundai. The contract has not been finalized. Hanwha Ocean has so far held talks with state-run Hindustan Shipyard on ship design.
Promises to be kept
The agreements remain nonbinding, and investment terms and construction dates are still open.
The larger risk lies in India's follow-through. The yard would take four to five years to build, Kim said, and until then New Delhi and Tamil Nadu have to keep paying subsidies, acquiring land and ordering ships through state firms. "Whether it keeps ordering ships as planned is the question mark," Kim said. "How binding that cooperation becomes is the biggest question."
The subsidies also have an end date. India's shipbuilding aid is scheduled to run until March 2036, so a yard finished around 2031 would have about five years of assured support. "The 20 to 30 percent subsidies offset the cost gap," Han wrote. "They do not resolve it structurally."
Labor is the other unknown. Wages are low, but the skills and production capability of Indian workers are "not yet proven,” according to Lee. Korean builders have also committed to a $150 billion U.S. shipbuilding pledge, and while financing is plentiful, it is "somewhat unknown" how many local workers can be recruited, he said.
Local politics is another factor to consider. Tamil Nadu signed the deal under a government that lost power in May, and neighboring Andhra Pradesh has since courted the project. The new state government has begun transferring land for the yard, though salt producers whose pans sit on part of the site have protested, citing the threat to livelihoods their families have depended on for generations.
The new chief minister, a former film star without a political base, needs central subsidies to land the investments his predecessor attracted, Kim said. "If the current government loses this, it is completely over." As for a move next door, he said, "HD Hyundai may choose not to invest, but the possibility of it going to Andhra Pradesh is zero."
He sees the salt producers' protest as a dispute over compensation that state agencies are negotiating. "It is very rare for the central government to withhold support for a good project in Tamil Nadu for political reasons," he said.
The first hard evidence will be the DPR, due by late April, which will put numbers on stakes, capacity and timing that for now exist only as intentions.
BY KIM MIN-YOUNG [kim.minyoung5@joongang.co.kr]
