world-2b743f026f.headline: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
world-2b743f026f.fulltext:
Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.
At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.
However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.
In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.
Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.
Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.
The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend Aden on the southern coast.
“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

NEW DELHI: Global capability centres (GCCs), initially set up by MNCs in India to tap skilled talent, lower operating costs and manage global operations more efficiently, are finding growing acceptance among Indian businesses too. From conglomerates to companies with overseas operations, domestic firms are creating dedicated centres to bring technology, finance and human resources under one roof, reflecting a shift towards centralised operations.
Top conglomerates including Adani, Tata and Mahindra, have adopted the model to integrate operations, standardise processes and drive digitisation across their businesses.
For better efficiency
While no specific number capturing the rising trend is available yet, multiple companies and industry experts confirmed to TOI that adoption is gathering pace across sectors.
India has 2,117 GCCs employing around 2.36 million professionals, according to the Nasscom-Zinnov FY26 report. Most are MNC-led, with mandates extending beyond cost arbitrage to technology, AI, engineering and product development.
Says Bhanu Prakash Kalmath SJ, healthcare industry leader, Grant Thornton Bharat: As businesses become more global, digitally intensive and organisationally complex, dedicated capability centres can give strategic leverage and consolidate functions otherwise dispersed across business units or external providers, while building common technology platforms, retaining institutional knowledge, strengthening innovation and creating deeper pools of specialist talent, while delivering efficiency''.
Indian conglomerates, which have global operations have also been adopting the model to drive up efficiency and competitive advantage, adds Shalini Pillay, India leader - GCC, KPMG India. The trend is also spread to mid-sized companies with service providers helping them to establish and scale such centres.
Some groups are taking this a step further by commercialising capabilities developed for captive internal use. For instance, Strides Pharma's Arcolab, which began as a captive shared-services organisation, evolved into Pivot Path recently.
Companies such as ITC, Tata Steel and the JSW Group have captive shared-services centres supporting their wider businesses. Separately, ITC Infotech has set up a Future Capability Centre for a UK-based client, and is helping other companies establish GCCs.
Further, the pharmaceutical sector has adopted the trend, particularly among domestic companies with sizeable international operations. Domestic companies are increasingly exploring the GCC model to achieve scale and tap into innovation, taking a cue from MNCs that have expanded their GCC operations, said Sujay Shetty, global health industries advisory leader, PwC India.

Applications are open for the MCW Global Young Leaders Fellowship 2027. The Fellowship Program aims to mobilize young people with the skills and resources needed to create and implement vision plans in the areas of education, health, and economic security.
MCW Global’s Young Leaders Fellowship begins with the Community Needs Assessment – A one-month community needs mapping that prepares young people, between the ages of 18-26, from around the world to understand their local communities better. After the community needs assessment, Young Leaders participate in a 10-day intensive in-person training program that helps them become leaders of positive change in their communities. After the in-person training program, participants return to their communities to spend ten months developing their action plans with virtual support from alumni mentors.
Program Content
The program is based on three phases:
- Virtual | Community Needs Assessment (1 Month): The Fellowship begins with an intensive community mapping and needs assessment. Young Leaders will be provided with the tools and knowledge to assess their community. This phase is implemented prior to starting the in-person training, as it will give the young leaders a better understanding of the community’s needs.
- In-Person | Vision Planning & Project Development (10 Days): Participants come to the Fellowship with an idea of a community issue they want to address. Vision planning is the process of transforming passion into a concrete, tangible plan for change. Through the in-person training program, which includes diverse speakers, workshops, events, and facilitated group work, participants can put their local issues into a larger global context while understanding why they are uniquely positioned to change their community. Participants will also determine which tools and skills can be applied to an actionable plan.
- Virtual | Project Implementation & Alumni Mentorship (10 Months): To further develop and execute their actionable plans, Young Leaders are paired with alumni mentors, who will guide them in the in-person program toward creating an actionable plan. These mentors have gone through the Fellowship program and successfully graduated from it. During the year, alumni mentors support participants by facilitating quarterly “hangouts” and ongoing remote communication. Alumni mentors undergo customized training prior to the start of the program to support team building and cultural competency among the diverse group of Young Leaders.

indian-startups-a3d00cb47c.headline: India, US have agreed on preferential market access for Indian goods in America: Piyush Goyal
indian-startups-a3d00cb47c.fulltext:
India, US have agreed on preferential market access for Indian goods in America: Piyush Goyal
India and the US finalised the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February.
India and the US have already agreed that Indian goods in the American market will receive preferential market access compared to competitor nations, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Sunday.
India and the US finalised the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February.
The deal was to be signed earlier, but changes in the US tariff landscape have led to further negotiations on the agreement.
"This was already agreed between the leaders - President (Donald) Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi when they announced that we have both come to a broad framework agreement a few months ago and it has been acknowledged that India will get preferential trade access in the US with lower duties than our competitor countries," Goyal told reporters in Cairo.
He is here on a two-day visit to discuss ways to boost trade and investment between India and Egypt.
The minister was replying to a question about the US assurance that Indian goods will get preferential market access.
An official has recently stated that the US has assured India of a comparative tariff advantage over competing countries under the proposed bilateral trade agreement (BTA), with both sides working to conclude the first tranche by the end of the current financial year.
"We will have to see how the tariff framework unfolds. We are working towards closing the first tranche by the end of this financial year. Talks are going for the first tranche and the broader BTA," the official said last week.
The extent of the advantage to Indian goods, however, will depend on the tariff framework eventually agreed upon.
After the US Supreme Court struck down the Trump's reciprocal tariffs that were the basis of negotiations, the US is using alternate mechanisms to put up a new tariff architecture in place using provisions of the Trade Act.

global-economics-3a6267a1c6.headline: Bharat Semi raises $24 million in seed round led by Info Edge, South Park Common
global-economics-3a6267a1c6.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: Deeptech startup Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in a seed funding round led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures. The round also saw participation from Micromax, Valour Capital, New York-based Gaingels, and angel investors Mukul Agarwal and Karthik Sundar Iyer, the company said in a statement on Monday.
The funding will help the company accelerate the development of a new family of products, expand its engineering teams in the US and advance its go-to-market efforts with global customers.
“The fundraise will support the company for the next two-and-a-half years, until we become revenue-positive and have about six products deployed with some of our major customers,” Vrinda Kapoor, co-founder of Bharat Semi, told Mint.
The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in India's deeptech ecosystem. Mint reported on 1 September that deeptech companies had raised $2.3 billion across just under 200 deals so far this year, according to Tracxn, compared with $1.62 billion across 453 deals in all of 2025.
Betting on programmable sensors
Bharat Semi is developing programmable sensors whose functions can be customised through software for different applications. Sensors detect physical phenomena such as light, heat, movement and sound, and convert them into information that machines can interpret. The company is targeting sectors including surveillance, automotive, commercial unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and the Internet of Things (IoT).
As devices increasingly need to interpret their surroundings and respond in real time, the underlying sensor hardware is becoming more important. Vibhore Sharma, founding partner at Redstart–Info Edge's deeptech investment arm–and former chief technology officer (CTO) of Info Edge, said this was driving the need for advances in semiconductor hardware.
“This shift prompts a re-evaluation of the foundations of intelligence, particularly in the hardware at the edge. Bharat Semi is tackling a significant limitation in Physical AI at its origin, within the silicon itself,” Sharma said in a statement.
Bharat Semi initially targeted a seed round of $10-15 million but raised its target to around $25 million following strong investor interest.
“Deeptech requires a different funding approach from e-commerce. While e-commerce companies typically raise larger rounds as they scale, deeptech businesses often need more capital upfront, with requirements declining in later rounds. The shift is already visible, with average seed rounds rising from $1-2 million to $5-6 million,” Kapoor said.
Founded in 2021 by Kapoor and Vinayak Dalmia, Bharat Semi operates across New Delhi, Bengaluru and San Francisco. The company was valued at $149 million post-money as of January 2026, according to Tracxn. It had raised $4.63 million in July 2025, in a fundraise led by RedStart Labs and angel investor Ajay Upadhyaya, alongside two other investors.
According to the latest data from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, available through Tracxn, the two founders together held 94.2% of the company, followed by Redstart Labs with 3.69% and angel investors with 1.43%. These figures may have changed following the latest fundraise.
The company is pursuing customers in India as well as international markets, including the US and Europe.
“We are working with both global and Indian customers. It is a little difficult to get into the details at this stage, but Micromax is making a strategic investment as part of this round, which gives you an idea of where things can go. We have also had a longstanding public partnership with the US defence company General Atomics,” Kapoor said.
Bharat Semi's longer-term ambition is to own the entire technology pipeline, from the sensor to the application layer.
“We want to enable a world in which every device in every home and office can be built from idea to reality in a week. Our goal is to make technology and sensors so ubiquitous that even light switches in the future have our products,” Kapoor said.

india-deep-tech-cb3bba8f9d.headline: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
india-deep-tech-cb3bba8f9d.fulltext:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.
The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.
The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.
The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.
In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

global-economics-14f04cd6c5.headline: Sebi to issue AI guidelines for capital markets soon, focus on investor protection and human oversight
global-economics-14f04cd6c5.fulltext:
LivemintPublished15 Nov 2026, 04:10 PM IST
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) will soon issue detailed guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the capital markets, Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Saturday. The proposed framework will seek to balance technological innovation with investor protection, market integrity and financial stability.
Pandey said the guidelines would establish safeguards governing the use of AI by market participants. Key provisions are expected to cover disclosures, accountability of regulated entities and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach, ensuring that critical decisions involving AI systems remain subject to human oversight.
The regulator had floated a consultation paper in June 2025, proposing guiding principles for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) applications and models in the securities market.
The proposed principles aim to maximise the benefits of AI adoption while minimising potential risks to investors and the broader financial system.
Speaking at the inauguration of SEBI's pavilion at the 45th India International Trade Fair (IITF) 2026, organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), Pandey highlighted the growing threat of cyberattacks targeting financial institutions and cryptocurrency platforms.
He also flagged the increasing instances of digital fraud involving social media influencers, underscoring the need for stronger safeguards as financial services become increasingly technology-driven.
To address emerging threats, SEBI introduced a structured incident response mechanism in May this year. The framework is aligned with the Financial Stability Board's FIRE reporting template, which provides a structured approach to reporting cyber incidents.
Pandey said the regulator was continuously strengthening its cybersecurity infrastructure to respond to evolving risks and protect the securities market.
The SEBI chairman also highlighted potential cybersecurity challenges arising from advances in quantum computing.
He said the regulator was conducting an inventory of cryptographic systems and identifying areas where cryptography is being used to assess possible vulnerabilities.
According to Pandey, markets globally are preparing for the risks associated with quantum computing, with concerns expected to become more pronounced during 2032-35. He stressed that preparations must be completed well in advance to ensure that the financial ecosystem remains protected against future technological threats.
Pandey said SEBI has already developed several technology-driven supervisory tools, including its 'Sudarshan' platform, which is being demonstrated at international regulatory forums.
The regulator is also working to strengthen its AI capabilities through international initiatives and supervisory toolkits.
He added that SEBI was reviewing the existing regulatory framework to ensure that the adoption of AI by market participants does not undermine investor protection, market safety or the integrity of financial markets.
Also Read | Razorpay gets SEBI nod to raise funds via IPO
Separately, Pandey said SEBI has constituted a working group to examine ways to make the Innovators Growth Platform ( IGP) more attractive for startups.
The review will particularly focus on deep-technology and biotechnology companies, which often require longer gestation periods before generating profits.
The chairman acknowledged that the existing platform has not gained the desired traction and said the regulator was examining possible changes to facilitate earlier access to public markets for such businesses.
The proposed changes aim to provide investors with greater clarity about the risks associated with investing in early-stage companies while allowing them to participate in their long-term growth potential.
Pandey, however, declined to disclose details of discussions relating to budget-related matters.

world-2a2cc2900e.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
Eight arrests made in connection with an attempted arson, which Tallinn says was ordered by Russian intelligence.
Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia, after an attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blames on Moscow.
The foreign minister made the announcement on Sunday, after eight people were detained overnight in connection with an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
Estonian authorities said the attacks had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X, “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.
“Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.”
He did not specify how long the border closure would last.
A Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman told state news agency TASS that the plans were “yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia.”
Latvia’s Interior Minister Janis Dombrava thanked Estonia’s Internal Security Service on X, saying that several “Latvian citizens and non-citizens” were arrested.
“Since the collapse of the USSR, there have been people among us who are willing to commit serious crimes in Russia’s interests. We will continue our work to ensure that such people cannot endanger the lives of those who love Latvia and want to live in safety,” Dombrava wrote.
‘Shadow war’
Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state and a strong ally of Ukraine, currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.
Marko Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that the arrests demonstrated that Estonia was “prepared to respond swiftly to such attacks.”
“It is essential that Russia’s state-sponsored campaign of terror does not remain merely a matter of diplomatic protests, either in Estonia or among our allies elsewhere,” Mihkelson said.
“Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. European countries must respond with asymmetric measures of their own. Closing borders with Russia is one such measure.”

ai-4b562fd9af.headline: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
ai-4b562fd9af.fulltext:
Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.
A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.
The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.
The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.
The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.
Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.
“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”
A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.
IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.
The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.
Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.
It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.
Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.
The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.
Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.
“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”
Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.
“We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. But there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse. We have the knowledge and tools to make a difference.
“We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday (November 15, 2026) said Nvidia needs to “go outside the company” as it seeks a new chief executive after Jensen Huang abruptly stepped down last week.
Mr. Huang stepped down on Thursday (November 12, 2026) after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis.

world-c7e011fee4.fulltext:
Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
- Published
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.
The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.
Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".
It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.
The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.
Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.
As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.
Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.
The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.
Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

indian-startups-1193923d24.headline: Not Just About Temple: India’s Wearable Impasse
indian-startups-1193923d24.fulltext: “There is no established playbook for making wearables in India. If you have the capital, you can set up a team, hire a bunch of researchers and scientists and come up with a product and even start selling it,” a California-based Indian founder of a wearable startup told us this week. The heated and contentious battle on X over Temple has brought out a lot into the open. A lot has been said and written about Temple this month, and who’s right and who’s wrong. What has gone unanswered in the cacophony is what it takes to actually launch a health or fitness tracking wearable that’s made in India. Where do founders turn when they need their hypothesis tested? Which agencies are the most approachable and how much red tape can one expect? These questions are not just about Temple. It’s about any new device that’s being launched in India, whether it is looking to track blood flow to the brain or it is just a heart rate or fitness monitor. The distinction matters in a market where wearable manufacturers can build and sell products that track physiological parameters without necessarily undergoing the clinical validation expected of medical devices. For India’s wearable industry, the debate has exposed gaps in how companies develop, validate and market products that make health-related claims or even basic activity tracking. But first, let’s see where Temple stands before diving deeper into the ecosystem of health wearables. Temple’s Bet On Something New Deepinder Goyal launched Temple with a core proposition of tracking blood flow to the brain and entropy. The company set out to create two new metrics that give users something their smartwatches could never. Firstly, BrainFlow is said to track relative changes in the blood flow to the brain during everyday activity. On the other hand, Goyal has described Entropy as a measure of how hard the body works to shed heat. The company’s website says the metric captures the body’s load across thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive, emotional, pharmacological, postural, reproductive and recovery systems. However, research papers uploaded on its website clearly state that Temple cannot directly measure cerebral blood flow. In response to Inc42’s questions about how these are measured, Temple said the Brain Flow Index is a relative index derived from optical signals collected at the temple. The company said the index rose and fell alongside blood-flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery, a major artery in the brain, as measured through transcranial Doppler ultrasound. Temple said the metric currently has two applications in its fitness app. It helps users compare the intensity of their cardio sessions and sends prompts to move when their Brain Flow Index drops during long periods of sitting. Unlike heart rate or sleep tracking, which have been part of consumer wearables for years, Entropy is being positioned as a new physiological metric. Its scientific validity will depend on whether the underlying signals can reliably measure what the company claims. The fact that Temple is broaching new territory with these metrics is what has set alarm bells ringing. Founders we spoke to say most wearables already have algorithms available for the heart rate and sleep tracking that have been improved and enhanced over the years since the first such devices came about. “The real work comes when you develop a new tracker or establish a new biomarker or a new benchmark for measuring something new,” the founder quoted at the beginning said, adding that specialised algorithms need research papers and validation. This is why there’s so much scepticism around Temple in the medical fraternity, with many doctors accusing the company of pushing a product without adequate backing. Temple’s research page lists multiple studies examining its BrainFlow technology, including a study involving 23 healthy adults that compared its reading with transcranial Doppler (TCD), a clinical technique used to measure blood-flow velocity in major brain arteries. Another study compared Temple’s BrainFlow readings with near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), a technique that can distinguish blood volume changes in the brain from those in the scalp. The company says it has partnered with academic institutions across the world to study additional and more diverse groups of people, with further validation studies underway. Both studies are listed as being under peer review. A Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that validation work on Entropy is in its final stages and that it plans to publish the findings soon. Of Preprints And Peer Reviews After much criticism, on November 8, Goyal acknowledged the gap between the peer reviews, the studies and the launch of the devices, adding that the research on Entropy would be published soon. He also said BrainFlow was not the primary proposition behind Temple, but the starting point for its research. In an earlier November 5 post, Goyal said preprints would precede peer-reviewed publication and that further validation would continue as the product reached users. The distinction between publishing a white paper, uploading a preprint and completing peer review matters. But what do these words mean for founders who are entering the space fresh? Simply put, a white paper and a preprint make research available for public scrutiny, while peer review brings an independent assessment of the methodology, findings and conclusions. A second founder, an early stage entrepreneur building neuro-centric wearables, said credible validation requires controlled trials. “Generally, you need a double-blind test, a control group and a placebo group. The bare minimum that is respectable enough is 90 people.” However, there is no fixed requirement on the number of participants, they said when we asked whether 23 people is a large enough sample size for Temple’s study. “You can do it for 10 people. Nothing is a mandate. But is it respectable to have a big test group? Maybe,” the founder added. We were also told that publishing research papers is not compulsory either, but it helps establish credibility. At the moment, no regulations govern the release of such papers along with a product. “It’s not necessary to put out your research papers, but it is something that people demand for credibility,” the second founder added. Plus, getting a study peer-reviewed is not easy. Founders need to find the right testing bodies to conduct reviews. This comes along with a growing demand for independent validation from investors and others who want to partner with the startup. “Third-party trials are what most wearables get asked for, by investors and consumers. Even doctors are asking for them,” the founder added. For early stage startups, the cost of conducting larger studies can be a huge constraint. In their case, a study comprising just 100 subjects cost the startup around ₹15 Lakh, which the company claims is a lot at the early stage especially when the product has already been built. Most of the funds raised are depleted by the time the startup reaches the testing stage. Is Temple A Medical Device? The debate also raises questions about how India’s regulatory framework applies to wearable devices. Under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, a product’s classification depends on its intended purpose and the function it is designed to perform. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) regulates devices intended for purposes such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring or treating diseases, as well as investigating or modifying physiological processes. Simply calling a product a fitness or wellness tracker does not settle its regulatory classification. Its intended use, advertised claims and actual functionality matter when it comes to clearances. Some well-known doctors in the country, who are sceptical of Temple claims, said the device's capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. Hence, they have called for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators. However, Goyal has repeatedly maintained that Temple is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose or prevent any diseases. He has also said that the company will obtain regulatory clearance wherever required before making claims that need it. Responding to Inc42, a Temple spokesperson said the device does not diagnose, treat, cure, mitigate or prevent any disease, and makes no claims about any medical condition. The company argued that under Indian law, a product is classified as a medical device based on its manufacturer's intended purpose. It also cited CDSCO's 2026 guidance on medical-device software, which says software intended for general wellness, without any reference to disease, does not fall under the purview of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017. Temple said that if it ever intends to introduce a feature for a medical purpose, it will seek CDSCO approval before making it available to users. The Regulatory Road Uncertainty extends beyond how companies position their products into what regulatory clearances are needed. The second founder, who had earlier spoken about the importance of clinical trials and third-party validation, said their company obtained CDSCO approval despite not making any medical claims. The founder said the company pursued approval because it was developing a brain-focused wearable device. “In India, any brain wearable device needs CDSCO approval. Whether it is tracking blood flow or not,” the second founder claimed, adding that wearables targeting the brain face additional requirements compared with other wearable devices. “Even though I am not making a medical device, I have a CDSCO clearance. Because it is mandatory in India.” The approval process in this case stretched around 16 months from November 2024 to March 2026. We were told that before receiving approval, companies can test only a limited number of units in India, with CDSCO determining the permitted number. This also makes it harder for companies to continuously iterate and test. The founder was describing their company’s regulatory experience. However, CDSCO’s 2026 guidance on medical device software does not establish a blanket approval requirement for all brain wearables. The founder acknowledged that rules remain unclear for products positioned as wellness devices. They also pointed to gaps in enforcement, saying regulatory scrutiny is not always consistent. “The CDSCO is not very active in looking into such companies, unfortunately. This is a loophole in India that many exploit,” the founder said. A third founder said navigating regulatory requirements can be difficult for early stage startups, leading some companies to be over-cautious. “Here you need to play around with the regulatory parts. Because in India the regulations are very hard. The only reason we never say that it is a medical device is that compliance becomes very hard. Especially for a new startup.” The founder said companies need to be particularly careful about making claims related to detecting or predicting medical conditions. “So if we say we can detect, then it would be a medical device. So you have to play very carefully with the words.” The question, therefore, is whether wearable manufacturers are making claims that bring their products within the scope of medical-device regulation, regardless of how they choose to market them. Beyond medical device approvals, the founder also highlighted other certifications such as Wireless Planning and Coordination (WPC) approval for relevant equipment that allows wireless connectivity, and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification that are mandatory for electronic devices. Similarly, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) framework applies to relevant products marketed in the US and should not be confused with Indian regulatory clearance.
